title: The Biblical Truth About Dating: The Lie That Fearts Your Heart—and the Love That Leads You to Christ
paragraphs:
The Biblical Truth About Dating: The Lie That Fearts Your Heart—and the Love That Leads You to Christ
Before You Chase "The One," Read What God Actually Says About Love, Waiting, Purity, and Why So Many Hearts Keep Breaking
There is a question quietly echoing inside millions of hearts that rarely gets answered honestly.
"How do I know if this relationship is God's will?"
Some ask it after their third heartbreak.
Some ask it while secretly texting someone they know they should walk away from.
Some ask it because loneliness has become louder than conviction.
Others have stopped asking altogether because disappointment convinced them that God's timing must have forgotten their address.
The world has never talked more about dating.
Yet it has never been more confused about love.
Every day social media floods our minds with relationship goals, romantic fantasies, emotional advice, viral dating coaches, and endless promises that happiness is just one relationship away.
But beneath the polished photos...
Behind the smiling selfies...
Past the anniversary posts...
There are countless tears no camera ever records.
Broken trust.
Hidden addictions.
Compromise.
Manipulation.
Lust disguised as love.
People desperately trying to fill a spiritual emptiness with another human being.
Scripture does something astonishing.
It never commands Christians to date.
Not once.
Dating as we know it is a modern cultural practice, not a biblical institution. That does not mean it is sinful. It means it must be submitted to biblical wisdom rather than worldly expectations.

The Bible speaks extensively about holiness, wisdom, covenant, self-control, purity, sacrificial love, marriage, faithfulness, and the condition of the heart. Those timeless principles—not modern dating culture—must shape how followers of Christ pursue relationships.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not about asking,
"How close can I get to sin without crossing the line?"
It asks,
"How closely can I walk with Jesus?"
That is the difference between religion and discipleship.

The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly describe the heart as לֵב (lev)—the inner person, the center of thought, will, desire, and worship. Dating is never merely about emotions; it is about what captures your lev. Proverbs 4:23 declares:
"Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it."

The Hebrew phrase מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ (mikkol mishmar netzor libbekha) literally carries the sense of guarding your heart with the vigilance of protecting a priceless treasure. Scripture is not teaching emotional isolation but spiritual discernment, because every relationship shapes the direction of the soul.
The greatest danger in dating is not rejection.
It is slowly giving your heart to someone who is leading it away from Christ.
One conversation at a time.
One compromise at a time.
One rationalization at a time.
Many believers do not suddenly abandon Jesus.
They simply become more emotionally attached to someone else's approval than to Christ's Lordship.
That is why Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 6:14:

The Greek begins with Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (Mē ginesthe heterozygountes)—"Do not become unequally yoked." The word ἑτεροζυγέω (heterozygeō) describes animals bound together under the same yoke despite being fundamentally mismatched. Paul's concern is not social interaction or kindness toward unbelievers. His concern is spiritual partnership. Marriage—and therefore any relationship intentionally moving toward marriage—is a shared direction of worship.
Love cannot erase different masters.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:24 that no one can serve two masters. A relationship cannot thrive when one heart bows to Christ and the other does not.
Many people reply,
"But they are such a good person."
Goodness is not the Gospel.
Nicodemus was moral.
The rich young ruler was moral.
The Pharisees were outwardly moral.
Yet Jesus said,
"You must be born again."
The issue has never been whether someone is nice.
The issue is whether Christ has become King.
Real biblical love is never merely chemistry.

The New Testament uses several Greek words for love, but the highest expression is ἀγάπη (agapē)—the self-giving, covenantal love demonstrated by God through Christ. Paul describes this love in 1 Corinthians 13, not as an uncontrollable emotion but as a deliberate, Spirit-shaped way of living.
Agapē is patient.
Agapē is kind.
Agapē rejoices with the truth.
Agapē endures.
This is not sentimental romance. It is cruciform love—love shaped by the cross.

Our culture often celebrates feelings as the highest authority. Scripture teaches that feelings are real but not infallible. Jeremiah 17:9 warns that "the heart is deceitful above all things," reminding us that desires must be tested by God's revealed truth rather than enthroned above it.
This does not mean emotions are evil. God created them. It means emotions make faithful servants but dangerous masters.

Some relationships begin with overwhelming excitement but slowly produce anxiety, compromise, secrecy, isolation from Christian community, or distance from prayer. Those are warning signs that should never be ignored.

James 3 distinguishes between wisdom from above and wisdom from below. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy, impartial, and sincere. Those qualities should increasingly characterize a Christ-centered relationship.

If pursuing someone consistently requires hiding, lying, sexual compromise, manipulation, or neglecting your walk with Christ, the relationship is not moving toward biblical love, no matter how strong the attraction feels.
One of the most misunderstood passages in Christian dating is Song of Songs 2:7:
"Do not arouse or awaken love until it so desires."

The Hebrew verb תְּעוֹרְרוּ (te'oreru) means "to awaken" or "to stir up." The repeated refrain throughout Song of Songs is not anti-romance. It is pro-wisdom. Love is a beautiful gift, but prematurely awakening covenant desires outside their proper context often leads to deep wounds.
Modern culture tells us to follow every feeling.
Scripture tells us to steward every affection.
There is a profound difference.

Jesus never promised that following Him would eliminate loneliness. He promised His presence. Before Adam received Eve, Adam walked with God. Human companionship is a gift, but it was never designed to replace communion with the Creator.
Many relationships become unhealthy because two spiritually empty people expect each other to provide what only Christ can give: identity, ultimate security, forgiveness, purpose, and lasting peace.
No boyfriend.
No girlfriend.
No spouse.
No soulmate.
Can bear the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can.

The Gospel is the greatest love story ever told—not because humanity searched faithfully for God, but because God pursued sinful humanity. Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. That is grace. Not earned. Not negotiated. Freely given through the sacrificial death and victorious resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Every healthy Christian relationship flows from that reality.
You are not dating to complete your identity.
You are dating, if you choose to pursue marriage, as someone whose identity has already been secured in Christ.
When your identity rests in Jesus, you no longer need another person to validate your worth. You are free to love without making an idol of romance.
Perhaps your story carries regret.
Maybe purity was lost years ago.
Maybe divorce left scars.
Maybe you ignored warning signs.
Maybe you chose desire over obedience.
Maybe your heart still aches because someone walked away.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
Grace rewrites the future by redeeming sinners who repent and trust Christ.
That is why our theme remains so precious:
The cross is where shame loses its final word.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed adultery and orchestrated murder.
Rahab had a scandalous past.
The Samaritan woman had multiple broken relationships.
Yet God's grace transformed their stories—not by excusing sin, but by confronting it with mercy and calling them into new life.
That same invitation remains today.

If you are single, do not believe the lie that your life is on hold until someone chooses you. Your calling is to know Christ, become more like Him, serve His kingdom faithfully, and walk in holiness. Marriage is a gift, but Christ is greater than marriage.

If you are dating, ask difficult questions. Are you helping each other love Jesus more deeply? Are you pursuing holiness together? Are you accountable within a faithful local church? Are your conversations, boundaries, and decisions reflecting the Lordship of Christ? Is your relationship moving toward a covenant that glorifies God rather than simply satisfying personal desires?
If the honest answer is no, do not ignore the conviction of the Holy Spirit.
Conviction is not condemnation.
It is an invitation to life.

The Syriac Peshitta, written in Aramaic, reflects Jesus' command to seek first God's kingdom in language closely related to the tongue He spoke. While the precise dialect Jesus used cannot always be reconstructed from the Greek Gospels, the heart of His teaching is unmistakable: the Kingdom comes first. Every relationship must be viewed through that lens.

One day every earthly romance will end—either by death or by the return of Christ. But those united to Jesus by faith will enjoy eternal communion with Him. Earthly marriage points beyond itself to the greater reality of Christ and His Church (Ephesians 5:31–32). That is why no dating relationship should ever become more central than the Savior it is meant to honor.
So before you ask,
"Is this the right person?"
Ask first,
"Am I becoming the kind of disciple who treasures Christ above every earthly relationship?"
That question changes everything.
Not to shame them—but to lovingly point them toward the hope found in Christ. You never know how God may use one shared message to redirect a life toward Him.
One surrendered heart can become the beginning of generations transformed by the grace of Christ.
